questions.stem: A 34-year-old man presented with chronic, painless swelling of his right foot. He was usually otherwise well and did not take any regular medications. Seven years earlier he developed a small wound after dropping a heavy box on his right foot. Several months later he developed swelling of the dorsum of the foot. Since then there had been intermittent drainage of pus from an area over the second metatarsal. He had received various courses of antibiotic treatment without improvement. He had no fevers and his weight was stable. He was visiting from India, where he worked as a farmer. On exam, there was marked swelling and induration of the affected foot and a draining sinus tract. X-ray showed no evidence of osseous involvement.
questions.lead_in: What is the most likely pathogen?
questions.explanation: Madurella mycetomatis Eumycetoma (Madura foot) is a chronic subcutaneous skin and soft tissue infection usually affecting the lower extremity (typically single foot). Areas exposed to trauma are most commonly affected. The disease presents with nodular lesions and sinus tracts draining macroscopic grains. The condition may evolve over years. Trichophyton rubrum is an agent of dermatophytosis. Talaromycosis typically presents with diffuse papular lesions that demonstrate central umbilication. Talaromyces marneffei (formerly Penicillium marneffei) is endemic in Southeast Asia and is predominantly affecting patients with AIDS. The chronicity of the disease is not consistent with P. aeruginosa or S. aureus infection.
questions.source: Comprehensive Review of ID · Quiz 1 Q27

parts.text: Name two causative organisms. Both genus and species names required.
The GP wants to know if they have to worry about systemic disease. Yes or no, and why?

parts_raw.text: What are two causative organisms. Both genus and species names required.
The gp wants to know if they have to worry about systemic disease.  Yes or no and why?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Ancylostoma braziliense (2) Ancylostoma caninum.
b) No. Humans are accidental (dead-end) hosts for these dog and cat hookworm larvae. The larvae lack the collagenase needed to penetrate the epidermal basement membrane, so they remain trapped migrating within the epidermis, cannot complete their life cycle, and do not disseminate systemically. The result is a self-limited, intensely pruritic serpiginous cutaneous eruption without systemic infection.
c) The eruption is self-limiting, but treatment shortens symptoms: ivermectin as a single oral dose (200 mcg/kg), or albendazole (400 mg daily for 3 days) as the alternative.
questions.beyond_mandell: The provided chapter text is Mandell chapter 261 (Agents of Mycetoma) and does not cover cutaneous larva migrans; answer rests on established Mandell (intestinal nematodes/zoonotic hookworm) and standard parasitology teaching.

cohort_answer.text:
Ancylostoma braziliense, caninum
The larvae of most species cannot mature within the human host since humans are accidental intermediate hosts. The larvae migrate within the epidermis and lack the collagenase necessary to break through the basement membrane. The larvae produce an inflammatory reaction along the cutaneous tract of their migration.
Self- limiting, ivermectin, albendazole

questions.question: For the following parasites, indicate whether treatment is indicated and, if yes, indicate what the treatment is.
questions.question_raw: For the following parasites, indicate if a treatment is indicated and if yes indicate what is the treatment.
questions.model_answer:
a) Strongyloides (stercoralis): Yes — treat all infections (risk of hyperinfection). Ivermectin 200 mcg/kg daily for 2 days is first line. Exclude concurrent Loa loa before ivermectin in patients with relevant exposure, given risk of encephalopathy with high microfilarial loads.
b) Entamoeba hartmanni: No — nonpathogenic commensal; no treatment indicated.
c) Blastocystis hominis: No (generally) — usually nonpathogenic; treat only if symptomatic and other causes excluded, with metronidazole (or TMP-SMX/nitazoxanide).
d) Trichuris trichiura: Yes (if symptomatic/heavy burden) — albendazole or mebendazole; can cause dysentery, anemia, and rectal prolapse/proctitis in heavy infection.
